issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the abstract, methods, and results are based on randomized/dummy Qualtrics data rather than observed participant data. Inferential statistics from randomized placeholder data cannot test the hypotheses, estimate effect sizes, or support any substantive conclusions. As written, the empirical claims are not valid evidence.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.description: The manuscript gives incompatible accounts of when data collection and analysis occurred. It states that data collection had started and was completed before analyses, yet elsewhere says the results are simulated and will be updated after data collection. This ambiguity undermines the credibility of the preregistration and leaves unclear whether any analyses were conducted on real data before the analysis plan was finalized.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period... All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.supplementary

issues.description: Participants appear to have chosen their own condition rather than being randomly assigned. Self-selection creates systematic confounding between participant characteristics and experimental condition, so differences between conditions cannot be interpreted causally as effects of the intervention or identifiability manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The study is described as a within-subject design, but the reported data structure is between-subjects: different participants appear in different cells, the cell sizes differ across conditions, and each participant is counted once across the six cells. This contradiction makes the design impossible to evaluate and casts doubt on the correctness of the analyses.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.description: If the design is truly within-subject, the reported ordinary two-way ANOVA is the wrong model; a repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed-effects model accounting for within-person dependence would be required. If the ANOVA is correct, then the design was misreported. Either way, the analysis/design alignment is faulty.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.description: The primary dependent measure was changed from an actual donation of real money to a hypothetical self-report donation amount. This materially changes the construct from behavior under real cost to stated intention/preference, which may not replicate the original psychological process or effect size.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly treats exposure to prior research about the identifiable victim effect, or exposure to joint victim statistics, as if these manipulations directly induce "analytical reasoning" or a "calculative thinking mechanism." But neither manipulation directly measures or validates deliberative thought, and no manipulation check is reported. The operationalization does not cleanly match the theoretical construct.
issues.quote: Our first goal is to conduct independent (close) replications of the identifiable victim effect, particularly on debiasing the identifiable victim effect through inducing a calculative thinking mechanism... explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect means that participants would be presented with prior research about the phenomenon while participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.description: In the joint condition, it is unclear what donation and feeling ratings refer to: the identifiable victim, the statistical victims, both together, or the act of comparing them. This ambiguity is especially problematic for the added "perceived impact of donation" construct and for comparing the joint condition to single-target conditions.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s)... The joint condition group would also be required to fill up the questionnaire about the affective feelings experienced in the experiment.

issues.description: The replication departs from the original in several consequential ways: updated stimuli, online MTurk administration, no earned $5 endowment, hypothetical rather than real donation, additional measures in the joint condition, and applying the intervention to the joint condition. These are not trivial changes and could alter both the psychological mechanism and the observed effect.
issues.quote: Updated victim information... Intervention applied to the joint condition... Imaginary donation... No reward acquired from a pre-survey... Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: Despite documenting multiple "Different" design facets, the manuscript still classifies the study as a "close to very close replication." By the authors' own comparison table, the DV stimuli, physical setting, and contextual variables are different, and the IV structure is modified. Calling this a close/direct replication overstates methodological similarity and risks misleading interpretation of replication success or failure.
issues.quote: DV stimuli | Different... Physical settings | Different... Contextual variables | Different... Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.description: The manuscript claims the sample size was chosen for adequate power but does not report the key parameters needed to evaluate that claim in the main text: target effect size, alpha, desired power, sidedness, assumed model, planned exclusions, or how the final target N was derived. Without these details, the adequacy of the design cannot be assessed.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of “Power analysis of the original study effect”.

issues.description: The manuscript states that participants were excluded for prior knowledge and failed attention checks, yet the cell counts in the results sum exactly to the full initial N of 1000. This suggests exclusions were either not applied, not reported correctly, or the tables are placeholders. Counts excluded per criterion and any missing-data handling are not reported.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration... Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The participant source is inconsistent across sections. One section says the data are Qualtrics-generated responses for preregistration, while another says participants will be recruited from MTurk. This leaves unclear whether any reported sample characteristics come from real participants, simulated data, or a planned future sample.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration... Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform... MTurk workers as participants

issues.description: The manuscript does not specify the response scales, anchors, item wording, scoring procedure, or reliability of the feeling measures. It also does not explain how the "aggregated feelings" composite was computed. This prevents evaluation of construct validity and replication fidelity.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling... We made minor changes to the questions evaluating participants’ feelings to specify the emotion they experienced to the victim information they have just read

issues.description: The abstract claims support for the perceived-impact hypothesis and states that identifiable conditions had lower perceived impact. But the reported results only show a significant difference between the statistical and joint conditions; the identifiable-versus-statistical comparison is non-significant. The abstract therefore overstates and misstates the actual result.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicts that identifiable victims should elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims, but the reported significant difference goes in the opposite direction and does not even involve the identifiable-versus-statistical comparison. The manuscript nonetheless treats this as support, which is internally inconsistent.
issues.quote: 6 (Extension) | An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims

issues.description: The narrative interpretation of the donation means contradicts the descriptive table. Averaging Table 7 indicates higher donation in the identifiable than statistical condition, yet the text reports the opposite and assigns pooled means to the wrong labels. This suggests a serious reporting or coding error.
issues.quote: From Table 10, we noticed that there is a significant difference between identifiable and statistical victim condition, t(994)=-2.40, SE=0.13, p=.049, meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: The pairwise comparison reports a negative t statistic for "Identifiable VS Statistical" but a positive Cohen's d. Unless the effect size was deliberately unsigned, this is inconsistent and makes the direction of the effect unclear. The manuscript does not explain the sign convention.

The manuscript states that the identifiability effect was "supported" even though the reported effect appears to run opposite to the stated hypothesis that identifiable victims should receive more donation than statistical victims. Statistical significance alone does not support a directional hypothesis when the observed direction is reversed.
issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.

issues.description: The manuscript conducts a large number of separate significance tests on individual feeling variables (multiple main effects and interactions) and then highlights a single p = .045 result for the extension. No familywise error or false-discovery control is reported for this family of tests, raising the likelihood that the lone significant finding is a Type I error.
issues.quote:
Table 13

Summary of statistical tests for segregated feelings... Perceived impact (Extension) | 2 | 3.11 | .006 | [0.00,0.02] | .045*

issues.description: The manuscript compares the identifiable/no-intervention cell to a pooled composite of five conceptually different conditions using a t-test. Pooling heterogeneous cells obscures interpretation, changes the estimand relative to the original study, and is not equivalent to a clearly specified model-based contrast unless justified and preplanned.
issues.quote: contrast the mean difference of identifiable/no intervention on donation with the combination of 5 conditions (statistical/no intervention, statistical/intervention, identifiable/intervention, joint/intervention, joint/no intervention)

issues.description: Critical procedural details are outsourced to supplementary files and external links instead of being reported in the manuscript. As a result, the reader cannot determine the exact intervention wording, order of measures, attention check content, or timing from the paper itself. This impedes evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: The session of “Procedure” in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study. For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.description: Several key materials are not actually provided because links are placeholders. This weakens the manuscript's open-science claims and limits independent verification of the preregistration, peer review, and presentation materials.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>

issues.description: The manuscript uses within-condition correlations between feelings and donation to assess whether feelings "predict" donation, but such correlations cannot establish that affective feelings cause donation. Reverse causation and common-method variance are equally plausible, especially when both variables are self-reports collected at the same time.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: The theoretical framing and implications concern real helping and charitable behavior, yet the replication uses hypothetical donation judgments in an online platform with a substantially changed context. Without stronger justification or acknowledgment, the manuscript overextends from stated intentions in a modified task to real-world donation behavior.
issues.quote: It can be reflected in our physical helping behaviour as well as donating responses... Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s)... Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform
